questions.question: A Lambda function with a 90-second timeout consumes messages from an Amazon SQS standard queue through an event source mapping. The queue still uses the default visibility timeout of 30 seconds. CloudWatch shows that many messages are processed successfully but are delivered to the function again shortly afterward, and some eventually land in the dead-letter queue. What should the developer do to stop the duplicate deliveries?
options: Set the queue's visibility timeout to at least six times the function timeout
Convert the queue to a FIFO queue so that SQS guarantees exactly-once delivery to the consumer
Reduce the function timeout to 15 seconds so processing finishes before the default visibility timeout expires
Enable ReportBatchItemFailures in the event source mapping's FunctionResponseTypes
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option A. Option A is correct because the messages become visible again after 30 seconds while the function is still working on them. Lambda's guidance is to set the queue visibility timeout to at least six times the function timeout so in-flight messages stay hidden, even when invocations are retried after throttling. Option B is incorrect because FIFO queues also use a visibility timeout and redeliver a message when it expires. Deduplication only applies to messages sent within the deduplication interval, not to redelivery after a timeout. Option C is incorrect because the work legitimately needs up to 90 seconds, so shortening the timeout would cause valid invocations to fail and the messages would still be retried. Option D is incorrect because partial batch responses control which messages of a failed batch are returned to the queue. They do not keep in-flight messages hidden longer than the visibility timeout. Key takeaway: A message is redelivered whenever the visibility timeout expires before the consumer deletes it, so the queue's timeout must comfortably exceed the function timeout (AWS recommends six times).

questions.question: A Lambda function processes SQS standard-queue messages in batches of 10 and calls a payment provider that is not idempotent. When one malformed message causes an exception, all 10 messages return to the queue and the nine valid ones are charged again. The team wants only the failed message to be retried and wants to keep the batch size at 10. Which change meets these requirements?
options: Set the event source mapping's BatchSize to 1 so that each invocation handles a single message and only the failing message is retried
Enable ReportBatchItemFailures on the event source mapping and return the failed message's ID in batchItemFailures
Increase the queue's visibility timeout so that the failed batch stays hidden for longer
Configure a dead-letter queue on the Lambda function that uses an on-failure destination, so that failed messages are captured separately
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option B. Option A is incorrect because this avoids the problem only by giving up batching, which contradicts the requirement to keep the batch size at 10 and reduces throughput. Option B is correct because with partial batch responses Lambda deletes the messages that were not reported as failed and returns only the reported ones to the queue, so the valid messages are not reprocessed and the batch size stays at 10. Option C is incorrect because a longer visibility timeout only delays the redelivery. When it expires, the entire batch, including the valid messages, is still delivered again. Option D is incorrect because function-level dead-letter queues and destinations apply to asynchronous invocations. For an SQS event source, failed messages are handled by the source queue's redrive policy, and this would not prevent the whole batch from being retried. Key takeaway: By default a Lambda error returns the whole SQS batch to the queue. Partial batch responses (ReportBatchItemFailures) make Lambda return only the messages you identify as failed.

questions.question: An IoT platform stores sensor readings in a DynamoDB table that uses provisioned capacity with auto scaling. The partition key is region (five possible values) and the sort key is readingTime. During peaks, writes are throttled with ProvisionedThroughputExceededException even though consumed capacity across the table is well below the provisioned amount. The application must still retrieve one device's readings for a time range. Which key design change should the developer make?
options: Use deviceId as the partition key and readingTime as the sort key
Use readingTime as the partition key and deviceId as the sort key
Increase the table's provisioned write capacity units
Keep region as the partition key and add a global secondary index with deviceId as its partition key
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option A. Option A is correct because a high-cardinality partition key spreads writes across many partitions, and the deviceId and readingTime pair still supports a Query for one device over a time range. Option B is incorrect because timestamps are written in order, so all current writes hit the same partition, and querying one device over time would require scanning many partitions. Option C is incorrect because capacity is divided across partitions and each partition has its own throughput ceiling. More table-level capacity does not help when a few partition key values receive most of the traffic. Option D is incorrect because every write still lands on one of five hot base-table partitions, so throttling continues. The index only adds a second copy of each write. Key takeaway: Choose a partition key with many distinct values and even access patterns; low-cardinality keys such as region create hot partitions that throttle even when table-level capacity is available.

questions.question: A developer adds a global secondary index (GSI) with customerId as its partition key to an orders table whose partition key is orderId. Immediately after writing an order, the application queries the GSI with ConsistentRead set to true so that it sees the new order. The call fails with a ValidationException. What should the developer do so that the application can guarantee it reads the order it just wrote?
options: Enable DynamoDB Streams so that the GSI query reflects committed writes
Increase the read capacity of the GSI so that it catches up before the query runs
Read the order from the base table by using GetItem with ConsistentRead set to true
Recreate the index as a local secondary index, which supports strongly consistent reads
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option C. Option A is incorrect because Streams record item changes for consumers and do not change the consistency model of index queries. Option B is incorrect because capacity affects throttling, not consistency. GSIs do not support strongly consistent reads at any capacity. Option C is correct because strongly consistent reads are supported on the base table, and the application already knows the orderId it just wrote. Option D is incorrect because a local secondary index must use the same partition key as the base table (orderId) and can only be created when the table is created, so it cannot index by customerId. Key takeaway: Global secondary indexes are eventually consistent only. If read-after-write guarantees matter, read from the base table with ConsistentRead.

questions.question: A payment service must decrement a balance on an item in an Accounts table and insert a matching record into a Ledger table. Either both changes must be applied or neither may be applied, even if the Lambda function fails between the two operations. Which DynamoDB API call should the developer use?
options: An Update on the account and a DynamoDB Streams consumer that writes the ledger record afterward
TransactWriteItems with an Update action for the account and a Put action for the ledger record
BatchWriteItem with PutRequest entries for the account and the ledger record
A conditional UpdateItem on the account followed by a separate PutItem on the ledger
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option B. Option A is incorrect because the stream consumer runs asynchronously and could fail or lag, so the ledger record is only eventually written. Option B is correct because transactions provide all-or-nothing behavior across multiple items and tables in a single request. Option C is incorrect because BatchWriteItem is not atomic, can return UnprocessedItems after a partial success, and does not support update expressions. Option D is incorrect because two independent calls leave a window in which the first succeeds and the second does not, so the changes are not atomic. Key takeaway: Use TransactWriteItems (or TransactGetItems) when several items must succeed or fail together; batch operations are for throughput, not atomicity.

questions.question: Two Lambda functions read an inventory item, compute a new quantity, and write it back with UpdateItem. Occasionally one function's write silently overwrites the other's, causing lost updates. The team wants a writer to detect that the item changed since it was read, so it can re-read and retry, without introducing a separate locking service. Which approach meets this requirement?
options: Read the item with ConsistentRead set to true immediately before every write, so that each writer always starts from the latest committed value
Use ReturnValues set to ALL_OLD on UpdateItem and compare the old and new values in application code to detect a conflicting write
Wrap each update in a TransactWriteItems call that contains a single Update action and no condition expression, so that writes are serialized
Store a version attribute, update with a condition that the version equals the value that was read, and retry on ConditionalCheckFailedException
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option D. Option A is incorrect because a strongly consistent read returns the latest data at that instant, but another writer can still change the item between the read and the write, so lost updates remain possible. Option B is incorrect because the comparison happens after the write has already been applied, so the overwritten data cannot be protected. Option C is incorrect because a transaction without a condition still writes the value the client computed from its stale read, so the last writer wins. Option D is correct because the conditional write is evaluated atomically by DynamoDB, so a stale writer is rejected and can re-read the item (optimistic locking). Key takeaway: Optimistic locking in DynamoDB is implemented with a version attribute and a condition expression; the database rejects the write if the item changed after it was read.

questions.question: A producer writes clickstream events to a Kinesis data stream with eight provisioned shards by using PutRecords. Every record uses the partition key "web". CloudWatch shows WriteProvisionedThroughputExceeded on one shard while the other seven are nearly idle, and some records in each PutRecords response fail with ProvisionedThroughputExceededException. Which TWO actions should the developer take? (Select TWO)
options: Use a high-cardinality partition key, such as a session ID, so that records are distributed across all shards
Use UpdateShardCount to double the number of shards and keep the partition key unchanged
Increase the stream's data retention period to seven days
Enable enhanced fan-out for the consumer applications
Resend only the records that are reported as failed in the PutRecords response, using exponential backoff
questions.explanation: Correct answers: Option A and Option E. Option A is correct because Kinesis maps the partition key to a shard by hashing, so a single constant key sends every record to one shard regardless of how many shards exist. Option B is incorrect because records with the same partition key always hash to the same hash key value, so they still map to a single shard after resharding. Option C is incorrect because retention determines how long records are kept and has no effect on per-shard write limits. Option D is incorrect because enhanced fan-out increases read throughput per consumer. The problem is on the write path. Option E is correct because PutRecords can partially succeed. Retrying only the failed records with backoff is the documented way to handle throttled writes without duplicating the successful ones. Key takeaway: A hot shard is a key-design problem, not a capacity problem: the partition key must vary. Producers must also handle partial failures by retrying only the failed records.

questions.question: A Lambda function reads a Kinesis data stream through an event source mapping with a batch size of 500. One malformed record makes the function fail on every attempt, so processing of the shard is stuck and the iterator age keeps growing. The team wants the bad record isolated automatically, wants processing to move on after a bounded number of attempts, and wants metadata about the discarded records kept for later analysis. Which THREE settings should the developer configure on the event source mapping? (Select THREE)
options: Set MaximumRetryAttempts (and, optionally, MaximumRecordAgeInSeconds) to a finite value
Set ParallelizationFactor to 10
Enable BisectBatchOnFunctionError
Configure an on-failure destination such as an SQS queue or SNS topic
Configure a dead-letter queue on the Lambda function
questions.explanation: Correct answers: Option A, Option C, and Option D. Option A is correct because by default Lambda retries until the records expire, which blocks the shard. Finite limits let processing move past the failing records. Option B is incorrect because a higher parallelization factor processes more batches from a shard concurrently, but the failing batch is still retried without limit and no metadata is kept. Option C is correct because Lambda splits a failing batch in two and retries each half, which isolates the malformed record from the healthy ones. Option D is correct because records that exhaust the retry limits are discarded, and the destination receives metadata about the failed batch, including the shard and sequence number range, for later analysis. Option E is incorrect because function-level dead-letter queues apply to asynchronous invocations. Stream event source mappings use an on-failure destination configured on the mapping. Key takeaway: For stream sources, combine batch bisecting, bounded retries or record age, and an on-failure destination to keep a poison record from blocking a shard.

questions.question: An S3 upload asynchronously invokes a Lambda function. After each invocation the team needs to send the function's return value to a Step Functions state machine when it succeeds, and the error details to an SQS queue when it fails after all retries. Which configuration meets these requirements?
options: Configure two S3 event notifications for the same upload, one for Step Functions and one for SQS
Invoke the function synchronously and inspect the response's status code and payload in the caller
Configure an on-success destination and an on-failure destination in the function's asynchronous invocation settings
Configure a dead-letter queue on the function and poll it for both successful and failed events
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option C. Option A is incorrect because S3 does not know the outcome of the Lambda invocation, so both targets would receive the event regardless of success or failure. Option B is incorrect because S3 notifications invoke Lambda asynchronously, so there is no caller that receives the function's response. Option C is correct because destinations route the invocation record, including the response on success and the error on failure, to the target that you choose for each outcome. Option D is incorrect because a dead-letter queue only receives events that failed after retries, and it contains the original event rather than the function's response. Key takeaway: Lambda destinations replace much of the DLQ pattern for asynchronous invocations: they support both success and failure outcomes and carry the response or error details.

questions.question: A Lambda function is attached to two private subnets so that it can reach an Amazon RDS instance. Since the change, the function times out when it writes to a DynamoDB table and when it calls a partner's public HTTPS API. The subnets' route tables contain only the local VPC route. Security policy requires that DynamoDB traffic not traverse the public internet. Which TWO changes will fix the timeouts? (Select TWO)
options: Create an interface VPC endpoint for the Lambda service
Move the function to public subnets that have a route to an internet gateway so that Lambda assigns a public IP address
Create a gateway VPC endpoint for DynamoDB and associate it with the private subnets' route tables
Add an inbound rule for TCP port 443 to the function's security group
Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet and add a default route in the private subnets' route tables that targets it
questions.explanation: Correct answers: Option C and Option E. Option A is incorrect because this lets clients in the VPC call the Lambda API privately. It provides no route to DynamoDB or the partner's API. Option B is incorrect because Lambda functions attached to a VPC never receive public IP addresses, even in a public subnet, so they cannot use an internet gateway directly. Option C is correct because the gateway endpoint adds a route that keeps DynamoDB traffic on the AWS network without an internet path. Option D is incorrect because the timeouts affect outbound connections, and security groups are stateful, so inbound rules are irrelevant to the function's outgoing requests. Option E is correct because the partner API is on the public internet, and VPC-attached functions can reach it only through a NAT gateway (or NAT instance). Key takeaway: A Lambda function in a VPC loses default internet access: use VPC endpoints for AWS services and a NAT gateway for public endpoints.

questions.question: An order-processing Lambda function is invoked by API Gateway and by an SQS queue. It writes to a relational database that supports at most 60 concurrent connections. Other functions in the account share the Region's concurrency pool, and during surges the order function sometimes exceeds 60 concurrent executions while a reporting function is starved. The team wants to cap the order function at 60 and guarantee that this capacity is always available to it. Which setting should the developer configure?
options: Reserved concurrency of 60 on the order function
A maximum concurrency of 60 on the SQS event source mapping
Provisioned concurrency of 60 on the order function
A usage plan on the API stage with a rate limit of 60 requests per second
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option A. Option A is correct because reserved concurrency both guarantees that amount of concurrency for the function and acts as its maximum, and it applies to every invocation source. Option B is incorrect because this limits only the SQS-triggered invocations, so API Gateway invocations could still push total concurrency above 60, and it does not reserve capacity. Option C is incorrect because provisioned concurrency pre-initializes 60 environments but does not cap the function, which can still scale beyond 60 using unreserved concurrency. Option D is incorrect because a request rate is not the same as concurrency, it covers only the API Gateway path, and it does not guarantee capacity for the function. Key takeaway: Reserved concurrency is both a guarantee and a ceiling for a function; provisioned concurrency only controls pre-warmed environments.

questions.question: A Java 21 Lambda function that initializes a dependency-injection framework has cold starts of about six seconds. Traffic is spiky. The team wants to cut cold-start latency substantially with minimal code changes and without paying for pre-initialized capacity around the clock. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Enable SnapStart, publish a version, and invoke the function through an alias that points to that version
Enable SnapStart and keep invoking the unqualified $LATEST version of the function
Package the function as a container image so that framework initialization runs faster on each cold start
Configure provisioned concurrency on the $LATEST version so that initialized environments are always available
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option A. Option A is correct because SnapStart snapshots the initialized execution environment when a version is published and restores it on cold starts, typically without code changes and without a charge for idle capacity. Option B is incorrect because SnapStart takes effect only for published versions and aliases that point to them, so invocations of $LATEST get no benefit. Option C is incorrect because container images do not shorten framework initialization, and SnapStart itself does not support container images. Option D is incorrect because provisioned concurrency cannot be configured on $LATEST, and it would bill continuously for pre-initialized environments. Key takeaway: SnapStart reduces cold starts for supported managed runtimes (Java 11+, Python 3.12+, .NET 8+), but only on published versions and aliases, and it cannot be combined with provisioned concurrency.

questions.question: A REST API in Amazon API Gateway proxies POST /orders to a Lambda function. Clients occasionally send bodies that are missing the required customerId and items fields, and the function is invoked and billed just to return a 400 error. The developer wants API Gateway to reject these requests with a 400 response before the function is invoked. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Define a JSON schema model for the body and enable a request validator on the POST method that validates the body
Add a mapping template to the integration request that returns a 400 status when required fields are missing from the body
Migrate to an HTTP API, which validates request bodies against a JSON schema before invoking the integration
Attach a Lambda authorizer that inspects the request body and returns a Deny policy when the required fields are missing
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option A. Option A is correct because REST APIs can validate the body against a model and return a 400 response without calling the integration. Option B is incorrect because mapping templates transform the payload that is sent to the backend. They cannot stop the request from being forwarded to the integration. Option C is incorrect because HTTP APIs do not offer request validation. Request validation is one of the features that is available only for REST APIs. Option D is incorrect because authorizers receive headers, query strings, and context but not the request body, and each authorizer invocation is itself a billed Lambda call. Key takeaway: Use API Gateway request validators with models (REST APIs) to reject malformed requests before they reach the backend.

questions.question: A Python Lambda function is integrated with an API Gateway REST API by using Lambda proxy integration. The function ends with return {"message": "created", "id": order_id}. Clients receive a 502 Bad Gateway response, while the function's CloudWatch logs show a successful invocation. What should the developer do?
options: Switch to a non-proxy integration because proxy integrations cannot return JSON bodies
Return an object that contains a statusCode and a string body, plus optional headers
Add a resource-based policy that allows apigateway.amazonaws.com to invoke the function
Reduce the function's timeout below API Gateway's integration timeout
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option B. Option A is incorrect because proxy integrations can return JSON, provided the response has the required structure. Switching integration types is unnecessary. Option B is correct because with proxy integration API Gateway expects the function to return this response structure, and any other shape produces a malformed-response 502 error. Option C is incorrect because missing invoke permission would prevent the function from running at all. The logs show that the invocation succeeded. Option D is incorrect because an integration timeout produces a 504 Gateway Timeout, and the function completed normally. Key takeaway: Lambda proxy integrations require a specific response format (statusCode, headers, body as a string); a malformed response is reported as 502.

questions.question: A developer must process new items written to a DynamoDB table. Only INSERT events are relevant, each event must be enriched by calling an existing Lambda function that returns customer details, and the enriched event must be delivered to an SQS queue. The team wants to minimize custom polling and glue code. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Create an EventBridge rule on the default event bus that uses the DynamoDB stream as its event source and targets the SQS queue, with the Lambda function as a second target
Write a Lambda function on the stream that filters INSERT events, calls the enrichment function through the SDK, and then calls SendMessage on the queue
Create a Firehose delivery stream that reads the DynamoDB stream and delivers records to the SQS queue after a Lambda transformation
Create an EventBridge pipe with the DynamoDB stream as the source, an INSERT filter, the Lambda function as enrichment, and the SQS queue as the target
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option D. Option A is incorrect because DynamoDB streams are not events on an event bus, so a rule cannot use them as a source. Polling a stream requires Pipes or a Lambda event source mapping. Option B is incorrect because this can work but it is exactly the custom glue code that the team wants to avoid. Option C is incorrect because Firehose cannot use a DynamoDB stream as a source and does not support SQS as a destination. Option D is correct because EventBridge Pipes provides managed polling of the stream, event filtering, an optional enrichment step, and a target, with no custom integration code. Key takeaway: EventBridge Pipes connects a supported source (DynamoDB streams, Kinesis, SQS, and others) to a target with optional filtering and enrichment, without integration code.

questions.question: A loan-processing workflow must pause after a credit check and wait for a human underwriter to approve or reject the application. Approvals typically take one to three days. The workflow must retain its execution history for auditing and must resume as soon as the underwriter responds. Which TWO design choices meet these requirements? (Select TWO)
options: Create the state machine as an Express workflow to handle the high volume
Add a Wait state with a fixed duration of three days before the next state
Use the .sync integration pattern with the approval system
Create the state machine as a Standard workflow
Use the .waitForTaskToken integration pattern, pass the task token to the approval system, and have it call SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure
questions.explanation: Correct answers: Option D and Option E. Option A is incorrect because Express workflows run for at most five minutes and do not support the callback (.waitForTaskToken) pattern. Option B is incorrect because the workflow would not resume when the underwriter responds, and it would wait even when the decision arrives sooner. Option C is incorrect because .sync waits for a job run by a supported AWS service to complete, and it cannot wait for a human response. Option D is correct because Standard workflows can run for up to a year and keep a full execution history. Option E is correct because the workflow pauses until the token is returned, then resumes immediately with the underwriter's decision. Key takeaway: Use Standard workflows with the callback (.waitForTaskToken) pattern for long-running steps that wait on an external system or person.

questions.question: A Task state invokes a Lambda function that calls a partner API, which sometimes returns HTTP 503. In those cases the function raises a custom error named PartnerUnavailable. The team wants up to four retries with increasing delays. If all retries fail, the workflow must run a compensation state instead of failing the execution. How should the developer configure the state machine?
options: Add a Choice state after the Task that loops back to the Task while a retry counter is below four, without a Wait state between the attempts, and route to compensation when the counter reaches four
Set TimeoutSeconds on the Task state and rely on the default retry behavior of Step Functions to retry the failed task
Add a Retry block for PartnerUnavailable (IntervalSeconds, BackoffRate, MaxAttempts of 4) and a Catch block that routes to the compensation state
Add only a Catch block and set its ResultPath so that the failed Task is invoked again with the error output
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option C. Option A is incorrect because this retries immediately with no increasing delay, and it re-implements what Retry already does. Option B is incorrect because Step Functions does not retry failed tasks by default. A failure without Retry or Catch fails the execution. Option C is correct because Retry provides built-in exponential backoff for named errors, and Catch runs after the retries are exhausted to transition to a fallback state. Option D is incorrect because Catch transitions to another state and ResultPath decides where the error output is stored. Neither retries the same Task. Key takeaway: Use Retry for transient errors (with backoff) and Catch for fallback paths; combine them to handle third-party failures inside the state machine.

questions.question: A Lambda function calls a third-party fulfillment API. When the API is degraded, every invocation waits until its 25-second timeout, which exhausts concurrency and delays unrelated requests. The team wants a circuit breaker so that after repeated failures all invocations fail fast for 60 seconds and then probe the API again. Where should the circuit state be stored?
options: In a shared store, such as a DynamoDB item that uses conditional writes and TTL, or an ElastiCache cache
In a Lambda environment variable that the function updates by calling UpdateFunctionConfiguration when the circuit opens
In the /tmp directory of the execution environment so that the state survives between invocations
In a global variable in the handler module, which persists across invocations of the same execution environment
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option A. Option A is correct because all execution environments run in parallel and are stateless with respect to each other, so the circuit state must live in a store that they all read and update. Option B is incorrect because configuration updates are control-plane calls that are rate limited and recycle execution environments, so they are unsuitable for runtime state. Option C is incorrect because /tmp is also local to a single execution environment and is not shared between concurrent environments. Option D is incorrect because each execution environment has its own memory, so other environments would not see that the circuit is open, and the state is lost on a cold start. Key takeaway: Lambda execution environments are isolated and ephemeral. Any state that must be shared across concurrent invocations belongs in an external store.

questions.question: A session table enables TTL on an attribute named expiresAt. Items are written with expiresAt set to an ISO-8601 string such as 2026-10-01T12:00:00Z. Days later, expired sessions are still returned by queries and the item count has not decreased. Which TWO actions should the developer take? (Select TWO)
options: Create a global secondary index on expiresAt so that TTL can locate expired items
Store expiresAt as a Number that contains the expiration time in Unix epoch seconds
Increase the table's provisioned write capacity so that TTL deletions are not throttled
Enable DynamoDB Streams so that the TTL process has a stream to write deletions to
Add a filter expression on reads that excludes items whose expiresAt is in the past
questions.explanation: Correct answers: Option B and Option E. Option A is incorrect because TTL does not use indexes to find expired items. Option B is correct because DynamoDB TTL only processes items whose TTL attribute is of the Number type and contains an epoch timestamp in seconds, so items with a string value are ignored. Option C is incorrect because TTL deletions do not consume write capacity. Option D is incorrect because TTL does not depend on Streams. Streams only record deletions for downstream consumers. Option E is correct because TTL deletion runs in the background after the expiration time, so expired items can still be returned until they are removed. Filtering makes the application ignore them in the meantime. Key takeaway: TTL needs a Number attribute in epoch seconds, and because deletion is asynchronous, reads should filter out expired items.

questions.question: A developer uses the AWS SDK to call Query for all events that share a partition key. For heavily used keys the application processes only the first portion of the results, and the response contains a LastEvaluatedKey. What should the developer do to retrieve all matching items?
options: Call Query repeatedly, passing the previous LastEvaluatedKey as ExclusiveStartKey until none is returned, or use the SDK paginator
Use Scan with ConsistentRead set to true because Scan returns results across the whole partition, including items that share the partition key
Set the Limit parameter to a very large value so that the whole partition is returned in a single response, since Limit has no upper bound
Increase the table's read capacity units so that DynamoDB returns larger result pages to the application in each response
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option A. Option A is correct because a Query response is limited to 1 MB of data, and the LastEvaluatedKey is the cursor for the next page. Option B is incorrect because Scan is paginated at 1 MB in the same way and is less efficient for a known partition key. Option C is incorrect because Limit can only reduce the number of items evaluated, and the 1 MB response cap still applies. Option D is incorrect because the page-size cap is not related to provisioned capacity. Key takeaway: Query and Scan return at most 1 MB per call; loop with LastEvaluatedKey and ExclusiveStartKey (or use SDK paginators) to read everything.

questions.question: A retail company keeps its product catalog in DynamoDB. The search page needs full-text queries with typo tolerance, relevance ranking, and faceted filtering across several attributes, at high query volume. DynamoDB Query and Scan operations either require exact keys or read too much data. Which approach meets these requirements?
options: Replicate catalog changes to OpenSearch Service, for example with DynamoDB Streams or zero-ETL, and run the search queries against OpenSearch
Create a global secondary index for each searchable attribute and use begins_with conditions on the sort keys of those indexes to match search terms
Scan the table with contains() filter expressions and sort the results in the application code to approximate relevance ranking
Cache the results of each search term in Amazon ElastiCache for Redis and serve repeated searches from the cache
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option A. Option A is correct because OpenSearch Service is designed for full-text search, fuzzy matching, relevance scoring, and aggregations, and it can be kept in sync with the table. Option B is incorrect because key conditions match exact or prefix values and provide no fuzzy matching or relevance ranking. Option C is incorrect because a Scan reads the whole table and charges for every item read, and filter expressions provide no relevance scoring. Option D is incorrect because caching repeated queries does not provide full-text search, and the first query for each term would still hit the same limitations. Key takeaway: Choose specialized data stores by access pattern: DynamoDB for key-based access, OpenSearch Service for full-text search and analytics-style queries.

questions.question: A mobile app authenticates users with an Amazon Cognito user pool. After sign-in, the app must upload each user's photos directly to a prefix in an S3 bucket by using the AWS SDK, without routing the data through a backend service. What should the developer add to the architecture?
options: A Cognito identity pool that trusts the user pool, so the app can exchange the user's tokens for temporary credentials for an IAM role
Sending the user pool ID token in the S3 request so that Amazon S3 validates the token against the user pool
A user pool app client setting that returns AWS access keys and a secret key inside the access token after sign-in
A dedicated IAM user for each app user, with long-lived access keys that are embedded in the app and rotated with each app release
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option A. Option A is correct because identity pools issue temporary AWS credentials through AWS STS to authenticated users, and the IAM role scopes what those credentials can do. Option B is incorrect because Amazon S3 authorizes requests with AWS credentials and does not accept Cognito JWTs. Option C is incorrect because user pool tokens are JSON Web Tokens that carry identity and scope claims. They never contain AWS access keys. Option D is incorrect because long-lived keys embedded in a client application can be extracted, and managing one IAM user per app user does not scale. Key takeaway: User pools authenticate users and issue JWTs; identity pools exchange those tokens for temporary AWS credentials for direct access to AWS services.

questions.question: A REST API method uses a Cognito user pool authorizer, and the method has the authorization scope https://api.example.com/orders.read configured. The mobile client signs in and sends the user's ID token in the Authorization header. Every call returns 401 Unauthorized, while calls to a different method that has no scopes configured succeed with the same token. What should the developer change?
options: Configure the authorizer's token validation expression to match the aud claim of the ID token
Have the client send the user pool access token, which carries the scope claim
Replace the Cognito authorizer with a Lambda authorizer because API Gateway cannot validate ID tokens
Grant the API Gateway service role permission to call cognito-idp:GetUser for the user pool
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option B. Option A is incorrect because the validation expression checks the audience of an ID token and does not add or check OAuth scopes. Option B is correct because when authorization scopes are configured on a method, API Gateway validates the scopes in the access token. Without scopes, it expects an ID token. Option C is incorrect because API Gateway does validate ID tokens for methods without scopes, which is why the other method works. Option D is incorrect because the authorizer validates the JWT signature and claims locally against the user pool's public keys and does not use a GetUser call. Key takeaway: With a Cognito user pool authorizer on a REST API, send an ID token when no scopes are configured, and an access token when scopes are configured on the method.

questions.question: Users of a web app sign in through a Cognito identity pool and read their own records directly from a DynamoDB table named UserData. The table's partition key is the user's identity ID. Which statement in the authenticated role's IAM policy ensures that each user can access only items whose partition key matches that user's own identity?
options: {"Effect":"Allow","Action":["dynamodb:GetItem","dynamodb:Query"],"Resource":"arn:aws:dynamodb:us-east-1:111122223333:table/UserData","Condition":{"StringEquals":{"cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:aud":"us-east-1:example-pool-id"}}}

{"Effect":"Allow","Action":["dynamodb:GetItem","dynamodb:Query"],"Resource":"arn:aws:dynamodb:us-east-1:111122223333:table/UserData","Condition":{"ForAllValues:StringEquals":{"dynamodb:LeadingKeys":["${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub}"]}}}
{"Effect":"Allow","Action":["dynamodb:GetItem","dynamodb:Query"],"Resource":"arn:aws:dynamodb:us-east-1:111122223333:table/UserData/${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub}"}

{"Effect":"Allow","Action":["dynamodb:GetItem","dynamodb:Query"],"Resource":"arn:aws:dynamodb:us-east-1:111122223333:table/UserData","Condition":{"ForAllValues:StringEquals":{"dynamodb:Attributes":["${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub}"]}}}
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option B. Option A is incorrect because the aud condition checks which identity pool issued the credentials. Every user of the pool would pass it, so users could read each other's items. Option B is correct because the dynamodb:LeadingKeys condition key restricts access by partition key value, and the ${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub} policy variable resolves to the caller's identity ID. Option C is incorrect because DynamoDB resource ARNs identify tables and indexes, not individual items, so this ARN does not match any resource. Option D is incorrect because dynamodb:Attributes limits which attribute names can be accessed. It does not limit which items (partition key values) are accessible. Key takeaway: Fine-grained access to DynamoDB items is enforced with the dynamodb:LeadingKeys condition and policy variables such as ${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub}.

questions.question: A multi-tenant SaaS application runs on Lambda. For each request, the function calls sts:AssumeRole on a shared TenantAccess role and passes the tenant ID as a session tag named tenant_id. TenantAccess allows DynamoDB access only where the leading key equals ${aws:PrincipalTag/tenant_id}. The role's trust policy allows sts:AssumeRole for the Lambda execution role, but every call now fails with AccessDenied. What is the least change that fixes this?
options: Call AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity instead, because AssumeRole does not support session tags
Add iam:PassRole for TenantAccess to the Lambda execution role's policy
Add sts:TagSession to the Action list of the trust policy statement for the Lambda execution role
Attach a tenant_id tag to the TenantAccess role by using iam:TagRole
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option C. Option A is incorrect because AssumeRole does support session tags. It needs the sts:TagSession permission. Option B is incorrect because iam:PassRole lets a principal hand a role to an AWS service. It has no role in calling AssumeRole. Option C is correct because passing session tags requires the sts:TagSession permission in addition to sts:AssumeRole. Without it in the trust policy, the AssumeRole call is denied. Option D is incorrect because tags on the role resource are different from session tags that are passed at AssumeRole time, and they do not permit passing tags. Key takeaway: Session tags (used for attribute-based access control, such as tenant isolation) require sts:TagSession in addition to the AssumeRole permission.

questions.question: Account A owns an S3 bucket whose objects are encrypted with SSE-KMS by using the AWS managed key aws/s3. A Lambda function's role in account B has s3:GetObject in its identity policy, and the bucket policy allows that role. GetObject calls fail with AccessDenied, and CloudTrail shows a denied kms:Decrypt. Which TWO actions will let account B read the objects? (Select TWO)
options: Call CreateGrant on the aws/s3 key from account B for the Lambda role
Add a statement that allows the account B role to the key policy of aws/s3
Encrypt the objects with a customer managed KMS key in account A by changing the bucket's default encryption and re-encrypting the existing objects
Enable S3 Bucket Keys on the bucket
Allow the account B role to use kms:Decrypt in the customer managed key's key policy, and grant the role kms:Decrypt in its own identity policy
questions.explanation: Correct answers: Option C and Option E. Option A is incorrect because a grant can only be created if the key policy allows it, and the key policy of an AWS managed key cannot allow another account. Option B is incorrect because the key policies of AWS managed keys are read-only, so they cannot be changed to allow another account. Option C is correct because only customer managed keys have a key policy that can be edited to trust another account. AWS managed keys cannot be used across accounts. Option D is incorrect because Bucket Keys reduce the number of KMS requests that S3 makes. They do not change who is authorized to use the key. Option E is correct because for cross-account use, the key policy of the key in account A and the identity policy of the principal in account B must both allow the operation. Key takeaway: Cross-account use of SSE-KMS data requires a customer managed key with a key policy (and an identity policy in the calling account) that allows the other account.

questions.question: An application encrypts 300 MB report files before uploading them to S3. The developer calls the AWS KMS Encrypt operation with the file contents and receives a validation error. The developer must keep the KMS key inside KMS and must not send the file contents to KMS. What should the developer do?
options: Call GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintext and use the returned data key to encrypt the file locally, keeping the encrypted key in the file header
Split the file into 4 KB chunks and call the Encrypt operation for each chunk, storing the ciphertext chunks in order
Call GenerateDataKey, encrypt the file locally with the plaintext data key, and store the encrypted data key with the file
Request a quota increase for the maximum plaintext size that the Encrypt operation accepts, then encrypt the whole file
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option C. Option A is incorrect because this operation returns only the encrypted copy of the data key, which cannot be used to encrypt data locally until it is decrypted. Option B is incorrect because this sends the file contents to KMS, which the requirement forbids, and it would need a huge number of calls. Option C is correct because this is envelope encryption. The plaintext data key encrypts the large file locally, and the KMS key protects only the small data key. Option D is incorrect because the 4,096-byte limit of Encrypt is a fixed size limit and not a quota that can be raised. Key takeaway: KMS Encrypt handles at most 4 KB. For larger data, use envelope encryption with GenerateDataKey.

questions.question: A developer enables automatic rotation on a symmetric customer managed KMS key that protects data in S3 and DynamoDB. A teammate worries that existing ciphertext will become undecryptable and that applications will need to be updated. Which TWO statements about this rotation are correct? (Select TWO)
options: Rotation creates a new key ID, so aliases must be repointed to the new key
AWS KMS retains the earlier key material so it can decrypt data that was encrypted before the rotation
Existing ciphertext must be re-encrypted with the new key material before the old material is retired
The key ID, key ARN, and aliases do not change, so applications continue to reference the same key
The same automatic rotation setting can be enabled on asymmetric KMS keys and on keys with imported key material
questions.explanation: Correct answers: Option B and Option D. Option A is incorrect because the key ID stays the same, so there is nothing to repoint. Option B is correct because rotation adds new key material to the same KMS key while keeping the previous material available for decryption. Option C is incorrect because the old material is retained, so no re-encryption is required. Option D is correct because rotation replaces the cryptographic material, not the KMS key resource. Option E is incorrect because automatic rotation is supported only for symmetric encryption keys, and not for asymmetric keys or keys with imported key material. Key takeaway: Automatic KMS key rotation is transparent: same key ID and ARN, old key material kept for decryption, and no re-encryption or application change needed.

questions.question: A Lambda function connects to an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL database by using credentials from AWS Secrets Manager. The secret is rotated every 30 days with the single-user rotation strategy. During each rotation, a few connections briefly fail authentication because the database password changes while some clients still hold the previous one. The team wants rotation without authentication failures for clients that retrieved the secret just before the rotation. What should the developer do?
options: Increase the rotation interval to 90 days
Cache the secret value permanently in the function's global scope
Configure a rotation window so that rotation runs during off-peak hours
Change the secret to the alternating users rotation strategy
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option D. Option A is incorrect because this reduces how often the failures occur but does not remove them. Option B is incorrect because the cached password becomes invalid after the next rotation, so the function would fail continuously. Option C is incorrect because a rotation window only chooses when rotation happens. The single-user strategy still invalidates the previous password immediately. Option D is correct because Secrets Manager keeps two database users and rotates the password of the one that is not currently in use, so credentials that were retrieved just before rotation remain valid until the next rotation. Key takeaway: Use the alternating users strategy in Secrets Manager when clients must keep working across rotations; single-user rotation changes the only password in place.

questions.question: A developer creates a new S3 general purpose bucket in September 2026 and uploads objects by calling PutObject with the SSE-C headers (x-amz-server-side-encryption-customer-*). The same code worked for buckets that were created years ago, but every request to the new bucket now returns 403 AccessDenied even though the caller has s3:* permissions. What is the most likely cause?
options: SSE-C is disabled by default on new general purpose buckets and must be enabled explicitly with PutBucketEncryption, or replaced by SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS
New buckets require kms:GenerateDataKey for every write because all new buckets default to SSE-KMS, so the PutObject call is denied
SSE-C requests are accepted only over unencrypted HTTP endpoints, so the HTTPS endpoint rejects them with an AccessDenied error
S3 Block Public Access rejects any request that carries customer-provided encryption headers because it treats them as public requests
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option A. Option A is correct because since April 2026, new general purpose buckets reject write requests that specify SSE-C unless the bucket configuration explicitly allows it. Option B is incorrect because the base level of encryption for every bucket is SSE-S3, not SSE-KMS. The failure is caused by the SSE-C headers. Option C is incorrect because SSE-C requires HTTPS, because the key is sent with each request. Option D is incorrect because Block Public Access controls public ACLs and policies. It does not evaluate encryption headers. Key takeaway: S3 now disables SSE-C by default on new general purpose buckets (April 2026). Applications that still need it must enable it explicitly; SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS are preferred.

questions.question: A static site's assets are stored in a private S3 bucket that is encrypted with SSE-KMS by using a customer managed key. The team puts a CloudFront distribution in front of the bucket. Direct access to the bucket must remain blocked, and CloudFront must be able to read the encrypted objects. Which TWO configurations are required? (Select TWO)
options: Use an origin access identity (OAI) and grant the OAI's canonical user read access in the bucket policy
Enable S3 static website hosting and use the website endpoint as a custom origin
Configure CloudFront signed URLs for viewers so that S3 accepts the signed requests
Add a key policy statement that allows the cloudfront.amazonaws.com service principal to use kms:Decrypt and kms:GenerateDataKey*, with a condition on the distribution's ARN
Create an origin access control (OAC) for the S3 origin and add a bucket policy statement that allows the cloudfront.amazonaws.com service principal with a condition on the distribution's ARN
questions.explanation: Correct answers: Option D and Option E. Option A is incorrect because OAI is the legacy mechanism and does not support SSE-KMS encrypted objects. Option B is incorrect because website endpoints do not support OAC or private buckets, which conflicts with keeping the bucket private. Option C is incorrect because signed URLs authorize viewers to CloudFront. They do not give CloudFront permission to read from S3. Option D is correct because CloudFront needs permission to use the key to read SSE-KMS objects, and that permission must come from the key policy. Option E is correct because OAC signs the origin requests, and the bucket policy limits read access to that specific distribution. Key takeaway: Use origin access control (not OAI) for private S3 origins, and add the CloudFront service principal to the KMS key policy when the objects use SSE-KMS.

questions.question: A REST API uses a Lambda TOKEN authorizer with a 300-second result cache. The authorizer validates a JWT and returns an IAM policy that allows execute-api:Invoke only on the ARN of the method being called. Users report that the first call succeeds, but calls to other methods within a few minutes fail with 403 and then work later. The team wants to keep caching enabled to limit authorizer invocations. What should the developer change?
options: Set the authorizer cache TTL to 0 seconds so that the authorizer runs on every request and returns a method-specific policy
Return a policy whose Resource covers every method that the token may access, such as a wildcard on the stage
Add lambda:InvokeFunction permission for apigateway.amazonaws.com to the authorizer function's resource-based policy
Increase the cache TTL beyond 3,600 seconds so that the first policy is reused for a longer period
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option B. Option A is incorrect because this would fix the 403 responses by disabling caching, but that contradicts the requirement to keep caching enabled. Option B is correct because the cached policy is reused for all requests that present the same token during the TTL, so it must cover every resource that the caller may access. Option C is incorrect because missing permission would make every call fail, not just calls to other methods. Option D is incorrect because the maximum TTL is 3,600 seconds, and a longer cache would make the problem worse. Key takeaway: Lambda authorizer policies are cached per token, so a policy scoped to a single method breaks other methods until the cache expires.

questions.question: A Fargate task pulls its image from a private Amazon ECR repository and sends logs to CloudWatch Logs, and both work. The application code inside the container calls DynamoDB and now receives AccessDeniedException. Which IAM role should the developer update?
options: The task role that is referenced by taskRoleArn in the task definition
The ECS service-linked role AWSServiceRoleForECS that ECS uses to manage resources on the team's behalf
The instance profile of the underlying EC2 instance that hosts the task
The task execution role that is referenced by executionRoleArn in the task definition
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option A. Option A is correct because the task role provides the credentials that the application code in the containers uses to call AWS services. Option B is incorrect because this role lets ECS manage resources such as network interfaces and load balancer registrations on your behalf, and application code does not use it. Option C is incorrect because Fargate tasks do not run on instances that you manage, so there is no instance profile to update. Option D is incorrect because the execution role is used by the ECS agent to pull images and write logs, not by the application code. Key takeaway: Use the task role for application permissions and the task execution role for the ECS agent's image pulls and log delivery.

questions.question: A Java service on Amazon EC2 uses the SDK's default credential provider chain. The instance profile role allows only read access to S3. During troubleshooting last month, a developer set AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY for that developer's own IAM user in the service's systemd unit file. The service can now delete S3 objects, which the instance role does not allow. What explains this behavior?
options: Instance profile credentials take precedence, but the IAM user's policies are added to the instance role's policies
IAM users always take precedence over IAM roles during policy evaluation, regardless of which credentials signed the request
The SDK merges the permissions of every credential source that it discovers in the chain and applies the combined permissions to each request
Environment variables come before the instance profile in the default chain, so the SDK signs requests as the developer's IAM user
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option D. Option A is incorrect because instance profile credentials are not used in this case, and IAM policies are never merged across principals. Option B is incorrect because policy evaluation has no such precedence. The request is evaluated for the single principal whose credentials signed it. Option C is incorrect because the SDK selects one set of credentials, and it does not combine permissions from several sources. Option D is correct because the default chain checks sources in a fixed order, and environment variables come before container and instance profile credentials. Key takeaway: The default credential provider chain uses the first source that it finds; environment variables outrank the instance profile, so stray keys silently override the role.

questions.question: A CI role runs a deployment that calls lambda:CreateFunction and specifies an existing execution role named OrdersFnRole. The call fails with an error that the CI role is not authorized to perform iam:PassRole on OrdersFnRole. The CI role already has lambda:*. Which statement should be added to the CI role's identity policy to fix this with least privilege?
options: {"Effect":"Allow","Action":"iam:PassRole","Resource":"*","Condition":{"StringEquals":{"iam:PassedToService":"lambda.amazonaws.com"}}}
{"Effect":"Allow","Action":["iam:GetRole","iam:ListRoles","iam:ListAttachedRolePolicies"],"Resource":"arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/OrdersFnRole"}
{"Sid":"AssumeOrdersRole","Effect":"Allow","Action":"sts:AssumeRole","Resource":"arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/OrdersFnRole","Condition":{"StringEquals":{"sts:ExternalId":"orders-ci"}}}
{"Effect":"Allow","Action":"iam:PassRole","Resource":"arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/OrdersFnRole","Condition":{"StringEquals":{"iam:PassedToService":"lambda.amazonaws.com"}}}
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option D. Option A is incorrect because this would fix the error, but it allows the CI role to pass any role in the account, so it violates least privilege. Option B is incorrect because reading role information does not authorize passing the role to a service. Option C is incorrect because the CI role does not assume OrdersFnRole. The Lambda service assumes it, and passing the role requires iam:PassRole. Option D is correct because the CI role needs permission to pass this specific role, and the condition limits the target service to Lambda. Key takeaway: When a principal hands an IAM role to an AWS service (Lambda, ECS, CloudFormation), it needs iam:PassRole on that role, ideally scoped with iam:PassedToService.

questions.question: A Lambda function logs request payloads that sometimes contain customers' email addresses and payment card numbers. Compliance requires that these values are masked in CloudWatch Logs and that only designated auditors can view the unmasked values, without modifying the application code. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Encrypt the log group with a customer managed KMS key and allow only the auditors' role to use that key for reading logs
Enable AWS X-Ray active tracing on the function so that sensitive fields are stripped from the segments and log lines
Apply a CloudWatch Logs data protection policy with a mask action to the log group, and grant logs:Unmask only to the auditors' role
Add a metric filter to the log group that matches the sensitive patterns and replaces them with masked values in the stored log events
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option C. Option A is incorrect because encryption restricts who can read the logs at all. It does not mask values for the other readers who need to see the logs. Option B is incorrect because X-Ray records traces and does not mask log events in CloudWatch Logs. Option C is correct because data protection policies detect sensitive data and mask it in query results and log views, and only principals with the logs:Unmask permission can see the original values. Option D is incorrect because metric filters extract metric values from log events. They do not alter or redact the stored logs. Key takeaway: CloudWatch Logs data protection policies mask sensitive data without code changes; the logs:Unmask permission controls who can see the original values.

questions.question: A healthcare application stores patient notes in DynamoDB. Company policy states that sensitive attribute values, such as ssn and diagnosis, must never exist in plaintext inside the DynamoDB service and must be decryptable only by the application by using a specific KMS key. Which solution meets this requirement?
options: Require TLS for all connections to the DynamoDB endpoints and reject any request that arrives over an unencrypted channel
Enable DynamoDB encryption at rest with a customer managed KMS key and restrict the key policy to the application role
Use the AWS Database Encryption SDK for DynamoDB to encrypt the sensitive attributes on the client before writing them, with a KMS key
Add an IAM condition on dynamodb:Attributes that denies reads of the sensitive attributes for all principals except the application
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option C. Option A is incorrect because TLS protects data in transit, and the data is decrypted inside the service. Option B is incorrect because encryption at rest is server-side. DynamoDB decrypts the data with the key before it returns it, so the service handles plaintext. Option C is correct because client-side encryption means that DynamoDB stores and processes only ciphertext for the protected attributes. This SDK is the renamed DynamoDB Encryption Client. Option D is incorrect because this controls who can read the attributes but does not encrypt them, so the plaintext still exists in the service. Key takeaway: Use client-side encryption (the AWS Database Encryption SDK, formerly the DynamoDB Encryption Client) when the service itself must never see plaintext values.

questions.question: A developer creates a new Lambda function URL with the AWS_IAM auth type in a new account. A service in the same account, running under an IAM role, signs requests with SigV4 and receives 403 Forbidden. The role's identity policy allows lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl on the function's ARN, and the function has no resource-based policy. What is the minimal change that fixes the error?
options: Add lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl to the function's resource-based policy for the account root, because identity policies can never authorize function URLs
Create an interface VPC endpoint for Lambda so that requests stay on the AWS network
Change the auth type to NONE and add a CORS configuration
Allow lambda:InvokeFunction on the function in the role's identity policy, in addition to lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option D. Option A is incorrect because the premise is wrong. Identity-based policies can authorize a same-account caller, and the missing piece is the second action. Option B is incorrect because network path does not affect IAM authorization, and a 403 from authorization is not fixed by a VPC endpoint. Option C is incorrect because this removes authentication from the endpoint, which is not a minimal or safe fix, and CORS has nothing to do with a 403 from IAM authorization. Option D is correct because function URLs that are created after October 2025 require both lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl and lambda:InvokeFunction to authorize a caller. Key takeaway: New Lambda function URLs (from October 2025) need both lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl and lambda:InvokeFunction to authorize AWS_IAM callers.

questions.question: A team's CloudFormation template defines an AWS::DynamoDB::Table resource. A planned change to the table's key schema requires replacement of the table. Before executing the update, the team must be able to preview whether the production table will be replaced. If a replacement occurs, the original table and its data must be kept instead of being deleted. Which TWO actions should the developer take? (Select TWO)
options: Set UpdateReplacePolicy to Retain on the table resource
Enable termination protection on the stack
Set only DeletionPolicy to Retain on the table resource
Create a change set for the update and review the Replacement value for the table resource before executing it
Run drift detection on the stack before the update
questions.explanation: Correct answers: Option A and Option D. Option A is correct because UpdateReplacePolicy controls what happens to the old physical resource when an update replaces it. With Retain, the old table is kept. Option B is incorrect because termination protection prevents deletion of the whole stack. It does not preview or control replacement of a resource. Option C is incorrect because DeletionPolicy applies when a resource is removed from the template or its stack is deleted. It does not control the old resource during a replacement. Option D is correct because change sets show each resource change and whether it requires replacement, without applying anything. Option E is incorrect because drift detection compares live resources to the template and does not predict what an update will do. Key takeaway: Use change sets to preview updates (including Replacement), and UpdateReplacePolicy to protect resources that are replaced; DeletionPolicy covers deletion only.

questions.question: A CloudFormation template creates an Auto Scaling group whose instances install and start an application through user data, which takes about eight minutes. The stack reaches CREATE_COMPLETE as soon as the instances are running, before the application is ready, so downstream stacks start too early. How should the developer make CloudFormation wait until the instances finish bootstrapping?
options: Add a DependsOn attribute on the downstream resources that references the Auto Scaling group, so they wait for its creation to finish
Add a CreationPolicy with a ResourceSignal to the Auto Scaling group and run cfn-signal at the end of the user data script
Add an UpdatePolicy with AutoScalingRollingUpdate to the group and set a PauseTime that matches the bootstrapping time
Increase the Auto Scaling group's health check grace period to 600 seconds so that instances are given time to start
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option B. Option A is incorrect because DependsOn waits for the group to be created, which happens when the instances launch, not when the application is ready. Option B is correct because the resource does not reach CREATE_COMPLETE until the required number of success signals arrive, or the timeout expires and the creation fails. Option C is incorrect because UpdatePolicy applies to stack updates and not to the initial creation. Option D is incorrect because the grace period affects Auto Scaling health checks. CloudFormation does not use it to decide when creation is complete. Key takeaway: CreationPolicy plus cfn-signal makes CloudFormation wait for instances to report that bootstrapping finished.

questions.question: A SAM template deploys a Lambda function behind an alias named live. The team wants each deployment to send 10 percent of live traffic to the new version for 5 minutes, then shift the remaining 90 percent, and to roll back automatically if a CloudWatch alarm on function errors enters the ALARM state during the shift. Which SAM configuration meets these requirements?
options: AutoPublishAlias: live alone, which shifts traffic gradually by default
A DeploymentPreference of Type AllAtOnce with a PreTraffic hook that runs a smoke test
AutoPublishAlias: live with a DeploymentPreference of Type Linear10PercentEvery10Minutes and Alarms that reference the error alarm
AutoPublishAlias: live with a DeploymentPreference of Type Canary10Percent5Minutes and Alarms that reference the error alarm
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option D. Option A is incorrect because without a DeploymentPreference, the alias is updated to the new version immediately. Option B is incorrect because all-at-once moves all traffic immediately, so there is no gradual shift, and a hook does not monitor alarms during the shift. Option C is incorrect because linear deployments move traffic in equal steps every interval, and they do not send 10 percent and then the remainder after 5 minutes. Option D is correct because SAM creates a CodeDeploy deployment that shifts 10 percent first, then the rest after 5 minutes, and CodeDeploy rolls back if a listed alarm fires. Key takeaway: In SAM, AutoPublishAlias plus DeploymentPreference (Canary, Linear, or AllAtOnce types) with Alarms and Hooks gives gradual Lambda deployments and automatic rollback through CodeDeploy.

questions.question: An in-place CodeDeploy deployment updates a web application on EC2 instances that are registered with an Application Load Balancer. After the new version has started, a script must call the application's health endpoint and fail the deployment for that instance if the check fails, before the instance receives production traffic again. In which lifecycle event should the developer run this script?
options: BeforeInstall
ValidateService
AfterInstall
AfterAllowTraffic
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option B. Option A is incorrect because BeforeInstall runs before the new files are copied to the instance, so there is no new version to validate. Option B is correct because ValidateService runs after ApplicationStart and is the final deployment lifecycle event for verifying that the deployment succeeded, and it runs before the instance is allowed to receive traffic. Option C is incorrect because AfterInstall runs before ApplicationStart, so the application is not running yet and the health check would fail. Option D is incorrect because this event runs after the instance has been registered with the load balancer again, so a failing version would already be receiving traffic. Key takeaway: Order matters in CodeDeploy's EC2 lifecycle: ApplicationStart starts the app, ValidateService verifies it, and the traffic events control load balancer registration.

questions.question: A pipeline in a tooling account deploys to a production account through a cross-account role. The build stage succeeds, but the deploy action fails with AccessDenied when the production role reads the artifact from the pipeline's S3 artifact bucket. The bucket policy already grants the production role s3:GetObject. The artifact store is configured with the default aws/s3 KMS key. What should the developer do?
options: Create a customer managed KMS key in the tooling account, allow the production role in its key policy, and use it for the artifact store
Disable encryption on the artifact bucket so that the production role can read plaintext artifacts without KMS permissions
Replicate the artifact bucket to a bucket in the production account and point the deploy action at the replicated copy of the artifacts
Add the production role to the key policy of the aws/s3 key so that the role can decrypt the pipeline's artifacts
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option A. Option A is correct because cross-account pipelines require a customer managed key because the key policy of the AWS managed key cannot grant access to another account. Option B is incorrect because S3 always encrypts new objects, and disabling encryption is not possible or appropriate for pipeline artifacts. Option C is incorrect because this adds infrastructure and does not address the KMS permission that is causing the failure. Option D is incorrect because key policies of AWS managed keys cannot be modified. Key takeaway: Cross-account CodePipeline deployments need a customer managed KMS key for the artifact store, with a key policy that trusts the target account's role.

questions.question: A monorepo hosts several services. A team wants its CodePipeline to start only when files under services/orders/ change on the main branch, or when a Git tag that starts with orders-v is pushed, and not on any other commit. What should the developer do?
options: Add a first CodeBuild action that exits early if no files under services/orders/ changed, so that later stages are skipped
Keep a V1 pipeline and add file path filters to the source action's polling configuration for the services/orders/ directory
Create an EventBridge rule that starts the pipeline on every push to the repository and add a manual approval action after the source stage
Use a V2 pipeline with trigger filters: the main branch with a file path include of services/orders/**, plus a push filter for the tag pattern orders-v*
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option D. Option A is incorrect because the pipeline execution would still start and consume resources for every commit, and it would not filter by tag. Option B is incorrect because V1 pipelines do not support file path or tag trigger filters. Option C is incorrect because the pipeline would still start for every commit, and the approval only adds a delay. Option D is correct because V2 pipelines support trigger filters on Git branches, tags, and file paths. Key takeaway: CodePipeline V2 pipelines add trigger filters (branches, tags, file paths) and execution modes that V1 pipelines lack.

questions.question: A CodeBuild project needs a database password that is stored in the AWS Secrets Manager secret prod/db (JSON key password) while it runs integration tests. The password must not appear in the buildspec, in plaintext project environment variable definitions, or in the source repository. Which approach meets this requirement?
options: Define the password as a PLAINTEXT environment variable on the CodeBuild project so that the buildspec can reference it by name
Map a variable in env.secrets-manager to prod/db:password and grant the CodeBuild service role secretsmanager:GetSecretValue
Commit a KMS-encrypted copy of the password to the repository and decrypt it in pre_build with IAM user access keys that are stored as environment variables
Add the password to env.variables in buildspec.yml and restrict who can read the repository, so that the value stays inside the team
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option B. Option A is incorrect because plaintext values are visible to anyone who can view the project configuration. Option B is correct because CodeBuild resolves the reference at build time, using the service role, and injects the value as an environment variable without storing it in the buildspec. Option C is incorrect because a copy of the secret is still stored in the repository, and the long-lived access keys would be stored as plaintext variables. Option D is incorrect because the secret would be stored in source control, which the requirement forbids. Key takeaway: CodeBuild can pull secrets at build time through env.secrets-manager or env.parameter-store references, provided the service role can read them.

questions.question: A team runs a containerized service on Amazon ECS behind an Application Load Balancer. For each release they want 5 percent of production traffic sent to the new task revision for 15 minutes, with automatic rollback if a CloudWatch alarm fires. They do not want to create or maintain CodeDeploy applications or AppSpec files. Which configuration meets these requirements?
options: Use the CODE_DEPLOY deployment controller with the CodeDeployDefault.ECSCanary10Percent5Minutes configuration and an AppSpec file
Use the rolling update deployment type with the deployment circuit breaker enabled and a minimum healthy percent of 100
Use the ECS service's built-in canary strategy with a canary percentage and bake time, and associate CloudWatch alarms for rollback
Use the EXTERNAL deployment controller and adjust the load balancer's target group weights with a custom script after each release
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option C. Option A is incorrect because this requires CodeDeploy resources and AppSpec files, and the predefined configuration is 10 percent for 5 minutes. Option B is incorrect because rolling updates replace tasks gradually. They do not send a fixed percentage of traffic to the new revision or wait through a bake period. Option C is correct because ECS now supports canary, linear, and blue/green strategies natively, with bake time, lifecycle hooks, and alarm-based rollback, without CodeDeploy. Option D is incorrect because this makes the team build and operate the traffic-shifting logic that ECS provides natively. Key takeaway: Amazon ECS has built-in blue/green, linear, and canary deployment strategies with lifecycle hooks and alarm-based rollback, so CodeDeploy is no longer required for gradual releases.

questions.question: A REST API integrates with a Lambda function by using an integration URI that contains the stage variable ${stageVariables.fnAlias}. The dev stage sets fnAlias to my-func:dev. Calls to the dev stage return a 500 error with the message that there are invalid permissions on the Lambda function, although the function and alias exist. What should the developer do?
options: Replace the stage variable with a hard-coded integration URI, because stage variables cannot reference function aliases
Add a resource-based policy statement (Lambda add-permission) that lets apigateway.amazonaws.com invoke the alias ARN
Attach AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole to the function's execution role so that the function is allowed to run
Publish a new version of the function and update the alias so that API Gateway detects the change in the target
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option B. Option A is incorrect because stage variables can reference function aliases, which is the standard way to map stages to aliases. Option B is correct because when a stage variable supplies the function, API Gateway does not add the invoke permission automatically, so it must be granted explicitly. Option C is incorrect because the execution role controls what the function can do, not who can invoke the function. Option D is incorrect because the alias resolves correctly. The invocation is being denied because of permissions.
