Key takeaway: When a Lambda integration uses a stage variable, you must grant API Gateway permission to invoke each function or alias that the variable can reference.

questions.question: A data science team packages a Lambda function with pandas, SciPy, and a 700 MB machine learning model. Deploying the .zip fails with an error that the unzipped size must be smaller than 262144000 bytes, even after moving the dependencies into layers. The function must not be attached to a VPC. Which deployment option resolves the issue?
options: Mount an Amazon EFS file system and load the model from it
Upload the .zip through Amazon S3 instead of directly
Package the function and its dependencies as a container image stored in Amazon ECR
Split the dependencies across five layers, because each layer has its own 250 MB limit
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option C. Option A is incorrect because an EFS file system can be mounted only when the function is attached to a VPC, which the requirements exclude. Option B is incorrect because using S3 raises the limit on the size of the zipped upload, but the unzipped size limit still applies. Option C is correct because container images can be up to 10 GB, which is far above the 250 MB unzipped limit of .zip deployments. Option D is incorrect because the unzipped size of the function code and all its layers combined must stay under 250 MB. Key takeaway: A .zip deployment is limited to 250 MB unzipped (including layers); use a container image (up to 10 GB) for larger packages.

questions.question: A Lambda-based service must roll out a new pricing feature flag gradually to its callers, watch an error-rate CloudWatch alarm during the rollout, and automatically revert the flag if the alarm fires, all without redeploying the function. The function should read flag values with low latency and few extra API calls. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Store the flag in AWS Secrets Manager and use a rotation function to change the value gradually across the callers over time
Use an AppConfig feature flag profile with a gradual deployment strategy that monitors the alarm, and read it through the Lambda extension
Store the flag in a Lambda environment variable and change it by calling UpdateFunctionConfiguration when the rollout begins
Store the flag in a Systems Manager Parameter Store standard parameter and call GetParameter on every invocation of the function
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option B. Option A is incorrect because rotation is designed for credentials and not for staged rollouts of configuration, and it has no alarm-based rollback. Option B is correct because AppConfig supports gradual deployments with alarm monitoring and automatic rollback, and the extension caches the configuration locally in the function's environment. Option C is incorrect because each change creates a new function configuration that applies to all callers at once, with no gradual rollout or alarm-based rollback. Option D is incorrect because Parameter Store has no gradual rollout, alarm monitoring, or automatic rollback, and calling it on every invocation adds latency and API calls. Key takeaway: AWS AppConfig provides validated, gradual configuration deployments with alarm-based rollback, and the Lambda extension keeps reads fast and cheap.

questions.question: A production Elastic Beanstalk environment must meet the following deployment requirements: full capacity is maintained throughout the deployment, a failed deployment must not modify the existing instances, all traffic switches to the new version at once after health checks pass (no percentage-based traffic split), and rollback must require only terminating the new instances. Which deployment policy should the developer choose?
options: All at once
Rolling
Immutable
Rolling with additional batch
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option C. Option A is incorrect because all instances are updated together and briefly out of service, which violates the capacity requirement. Option B is incorrect because rolling deployments take each batch out of service while it updates, which reduces capacity, and they also update instances in place. Option C is correct because immutable deployments launch a temporary Auto Scaling group with new instances, and the existing instances are untouched. If the new instances fail, they are terminated and nothing else needs to be undone. Option D is incorrect because this keeps capacity by launching an extra batch, but it updates the existing instances in place, so a failure leaves some instances on the new version and rolling back requires another deployment. Key takeaway: Immutable deployments use fresh instances in a new Auto Scaling group, preserving capacity and making rollback a matter of terminating the new instances.

questions.question: A frontend team hosts a React application with AWS Amplify Hosting connected to a GitHub repository. Reviewers want a temporary, isolated URL with the built app for each pull request, and each preview must be deleted when its pull request closes, even if the source branch remains. What should the developer enable?
options: Web previews for pull requests in the Amplify app settings
A CloudFront distribution with one origin per feature branch
A separate Amplify app for every pull request, created by a CloudFormation stack
Automatic branch creation for feature branches
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option A. Option A is correct because Amplify builds every pull request into its own preview URL and removes the preview when the pull request is closed. Option B is incorrect because this does not build the pull request, and it would require custom routing and cleanup. Option C is incorrect because this is a heavy manual process, and the stacks would have to be cleaned up on every pull request. Option D is incorrect because this deploys branches that match a pattern. It is not tied to pull requests, and it would not remove the deployment when the pull request closes if the branch remains. Key takeaway: Amplify Hosting web previews build every pull request into a temporary environment and delete it when the pull request is closed.

questions.question: A developer is writing a Lambda function that is triggered by S3 ObjectCreated events. Before deploying, the developer wants to run the function locally with a realistic S3 event payload for a specific bucket and key. Which approach should the developer use?
options: Run sam local start-api and send the S3 event to the local endpoint with curl so that the function receives the payload
Run sam local generate-event s3 put with the bucket and key, then pass the JSON event to sam local invoke with --event
Run sam sync --watch so that S3 delivers real events to the function while the developer edits the code locally
Run sam validate with the --lint option so that a sample S3 event is generated from the template's function definition
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option B. Option A is incorrect because start-api emulates API Gateway endpoints. It does not emulate S3 event notifications. Option B is correct because the generate-event command produces sample event payloads for many AWS services, and sam local invoke runs the function in a local container with that event. Option C is incorrect because sam sync updates resources in the cloud and does not run the function locally. Option D is incorrect because sam validate checks that the template is valid, and it does not create event payloads. Key takeaway: sam local generate-event creates realistic test events, and sam local invoke runs a function locally against them.

questions.question: A developer runs cdk deploy for a stack that includes a Lambda function whose code comes from a local directory. The command fails with an error that the stack uses assets and that the environment must be bootstrapped. What should the developer do?
options: Run cdk synth first, because synthesis uploads the assets to an S3 bucket in the target account before deployment begins
Move the function code inline into the template so that no asset needs to be uploaded to the target environment, then redeploy
Run cdk deploy with the --hotswap option so that the assets are not required for the deployment of the changed function
Run cdk bootstrap for the target account and Region so that CDK creates the S3 bucket and ECR repository that it uses for assets
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option D. Option A is incorrect because synthesis produces the CloudFormation template and asset manifests locally. It does not upload assets. Option B is incorrect because inline code is limited to very small functions and does not resolve the need for a bootstrapped environment in general. Option C is incorrect because hotswap speeds up development deployments of supported resource changes, and it still uses the bootstrap resources for assets. Option D is correct because assets such as Lambda code and Docker images are uploaded to bootstrap resources before CloudFormation deploys the stack. Key takeaway: CDK apps that use assets (Lambda code, container images) require a bootstrapped environment: run cdk bootstrap once per account and Region.

questions.question: A developer must determine the 95th percentile of invocation duration, in five-minute intervals, for a Lambda function by using CloudWatch Logs Insights on the function's log group. Which query returns this result?
options: filter @type = "REPORT" | stats max(@duration) as maxDuration by bin(5m)
filter @type = "REPORT" | stats pct(@duration, 95) as p95 by @timestamp
filter @type = "REPORT" | stats pct(@duration, 95) as p95 by bin(5m)
filter @type = "REPORT" | sort @duration desc | limit 20
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option C. Option A is incorrect because this returns the maximum duration in each interval, not the 95th percentile. Option B is incorrect because grouping by @timestamp produces one row per distinct timestamp instead of five-minute intervals. Option C is correct because REPORT lines carry the duration of each invocation, pct() calculates the percentile, and bin(5m) groups the results into five-minute buckets. Option D is incorrect because this lists the 20 slowest invocations and does not calculate a percentile per interval. Key takeaway: Logs Insights discovers Lambda fields such as @duration on REPORT lines; use pct() for percentiles and bin() for time buckets.

questions.question: A Lambda function processes thousands of orders per second, and the team wants custom CloudWatch metrics (Count and Latency) with an OrderType dimension. Calling PutMetricData from the handler on every order adds latency and causes API throttling. Which approach publishes these metrics with the least added latency and without PutMetricData calls?
options: Buffer the metrics in memory and call PutMetricData once at the end of each invocation instead of once per order event
Enable X-Ray active tracing and use the trace summaries in the service map as the source of the metrics
Enable the Lambda Insights extension so that CloudWatch collects the order metrics from the function automatically
Write log events in CloudWatch embedded metric format to standard output so that CloudWatch extracts the metrics
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option D. Option A is incorrect because this still calls the API on every invocation, so throttling and added latency remain. Option B is incorrect because X-Ray traces are not CloudWatch custom metrics with the dimensions that the team defines. Option C is incorrect because Lambda Insights collects system-level metrics such as CPU and memory, and it does not publish application-defined metrics like order counts. Option D is correct because EMF log lines are ingested with the function's normal logging, and CloudWatch turns them into metrics asynchronously, so the handler makes no metrics API calls. Key takeaway: Embedded metric format lets functions emit custom metrics as structured logs, avoiding synchronous PutMetricData calls.

questions.question: A team has enabled active tracing on an order-processing Lambda function. They want to search traces in the X-Ray console for requests where customerTier is gold, and they also want the full request payload attached to each trace for debugging, without making it searchable. How should the developer record these values?
options: Record customerTier as metadata and the request payload as an annotation
Write both values to CloudWatch Logs and search them with an X-Ray filter expression
Record both values as annotations
Record customerTier as an annotation and the request payload as metadata
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option D. Option A is incorrect because metadata is not indexed, so traces could not be searched by customerTier, and annotations accept only simple scalar values. Option B is incorrect because X-Ray filter expressions search trace data and not CloudWatch Logs. Option C is incorrect because a request payload is a structured object and cannot be stored in an annotation, and annotations are limited in number per trace. Option D is correct because annotations are indexed key-value pairs that can be used in filter expressions, while metadata can hold any object but is not indexed. Key takeaway: Use annotations for values you want to search or filter on, and metadata for extra data you only need to see.

questions.question: A team is building a new Java microservice on Amazon ECS and wants distributed traces in AWS X-Ray. The architects note that the X-Ray SDKs and daemon entered maintenance mode on February 25, 2026, with end of support planned for February 25, 2027, and they do not want to build new services on deprioritized instrumentation. Which instrumentation approach should the developer use?
options: Add the AWS X-Ray SDK for Java to the service and run the X-Ray daemon as a sidecar container in the task
Instrument the service with OpenTelemetry, for example the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry, and send the traces to X-Ray
Enable VPC Flow Logs and correlate the flow records with application logs to build a trace for each request
Use CloudTrail data events to reconstruct the request traces between the service's components after each call
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option B. Option A is incorrect because this is the instrumentation path that is in maintenance mode and headed for end of support. Option B is correct because AWS positions OpenTelemetry as the primary instrumentation standard for X-Ray, and traces can still be viewed in X-Ray and CloudWatch. Option C is incorrect because flow logs record network metadata for IP traffic and do not contain request-level trace information. Option D is incorrect because CloudTrail records API activity in your account and does not trace requests between application components. Key takeaway: For new workloads, AWS recommends OpenTelemetry-based instrumentation (such as ADOT) for tracing; the X-Ray SDKs and daemon are in maintenance mode.

questions.question: A latency-sensitive function behind an API shows cold-start latency every weekday at 08:55, when traffic jumps from near zero to thousands of requests. Traffic is otherwise low. The team wants no cold starts from 09:00 to 12:00 and wants to pay for pre-initialized capacity only during that window. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Use EventBridge Scheduler to invoke the function every minute all day so that execution environments stay warm
Configure provisioned concurrency on the $LATEST version and schedule the increase for 08:45 with Application Auto Scaling scheduled actions
Set reserved concurrency to 1,000 for the function for the whole day so that capacity is guaranteed at 09:00
Publish a version, create an alias, and use Application Auto Scaling scheduled actions to change the alias's provisioned concurrency
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option D. Option A is incorrect because periodic pings only keep a few environments warm, cannot guarantee thousands of initialized environments, and run all day. Option B is incorrect because provisioned concurrency cannot be configured on $LATEST. Option C is incorrect because reserved concurrency guarantees capacity but does not pre-initialize execution environments, so cold starts still occur. Option D is correct because provisioned concurrency is configured on a version or alias, and scheduled scaling changes the amount to match the expected window. Key takeaway: Provisioned concurrency removes cold starts for the environments it provisions; use aliases or versions and scheduled scaling to control its cost.

questions.question: A CPU-bound Lambda function is configured with 1,024 MB. CloudWatch REPORT lines show a Max Memory Used of about 180 MB and an average duration of 2.4 seconds. A colleague proposes lowering the setting to 256 MB to reduce cost. What is the best way to find the setting that minimizes cost?
options: Run the function at several memory settings, for example with AWS Lambda Power Tuning, and compare cost and duration
Set the memory to 256 MB because Lambda bills per MB configured, and the function uses only about 180 MB at peak
Keep 1,024 MB and enable provisioned concurrency so that the billed duration of every invocation is reduced
Increase the timeout to 30 seconds, then lower the memory to the minimum that the function can start with
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option A. Option A is correct because CPU power scales with configured memory, so a lower setting can lengthen the duration enough to cost more, and only measurement shows the cost-optimal point. Option B is incorrect because cost is memory multiplied by duration, and less memory also means less CPU, so the CPU-bound function would run longer. Option C is incorrect because provisioned concurrency reduces cold-start latency and does not shorten the execution duration. Option D is incorrect because a longer timeout only prevents timeouts and does not make the function cheaper. Key takeaway: Lambda cost depends on memory and duration, and CPU scales with memory; measure across settings instead of sizing to Max Memory Used.

questions.question: An SNS topic delivers order events to three SQS queues. The publisher sends a JSON body such as {"orderType":"refund","amount":120} and does not set message attributes. The subscription for the refunds queue has the filter policy {"orderType":["refund"]}. The other two queues, which have no filter policy, receive every message, but the refunds queue receives nothing. What should the developer do?
options: Enable raw message delivery on the refunds subscription
Convert the topic to an SNS FIFO topic so that filtering can use the payload
Set the refunds subscription's FilterPolicyScope attribute to MessageBody
Add a queue policy that allows sns.amazonaws.com to send messages to the refunds queue
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option C. Option A is incorrect because raw delivery changes the message envelope and does not change how the filter policy is evaluated. Option B is incorrect because FIFO topics use the same filter policy scopes, and the default is still MessageAttributes. Option C is correct because the default scope is MessageAttributes, so the policy is evaluated against attributes that the publisher never set. MessageBody evaluates it against the JSON payload. Option D is incorrect because the other queues receive messages from the same topic, so delivery permissions are not the problem. Key takeaway: SNS filter policies apply to message attributes by default; set FilterPolicyScope to MessageBody to filter on the JSON payload.

questions.question: A CloudFront distribution serves a product API. Responses vary only by the lang query string. The origin also needs the X-Client-Version header and all other query strings for request logging, but they do not change the response. The cache hit ratio is low because the distribution currently caches on all query strings and headers. How should the developer configure the distribution?
options: Use only an origin request policy that forwards lang, and set the minimum TTL to 0 so that every request reaches the origin
Use the legacy forwarded values settings to whitelist lang and X-Client-Version in the distribution's cache behavior
Use a cache policy with only lang in the cache key, and an origin request policy that forwards X-Client-Version and all query strings
Use a cache policy that includes all query strings and X-Client-Version so that the origin receives every value
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option C. Option A is incorrect because disabling caching removes the benefit of CloudFront and does not address the hit ratio. Option B is incorrect because whitelisted headers and query strings are also added to the cache key, so X-Client-Version would still fragment the cache. Option C is correct because the cache policy defines what varies the cached object, and the origin request policy forwards extra values to the origin without adding them to the cache key. Option D is incorrect because anything in the cache key fragments the cache, which is what causes the low hit ratio. Key takeaway: Cache policies decide the cache key; origin request policies decide what else is forwarded to the origin without affecting caching.

questions.question: A team puts a DAX cluster in front of a DynamoDB table and points the application's SDK client at the DAX endpoint. Read latency for hot items stays at single-digit milliseconds, and DAX cache hit metrics stay near zero. The application calls GetItem with ConsistentRead set to true on every request. What should the developer do to benefit from DAX for these reads?
options: Increase the DAX item cache TTL so that strongly consistent reads are served from the cache for longer
Add more nodes to the DAX cluster and enable multi-AZ placement to improve the cache hit ratio for the hot items
Replace GetItem with Query on the base table, because DAX caches the results of strongly consistent Query requests but not GetItem
Use eventually consistent reads where slightly stale data is acceptable, because DAX does not cache strongly consistent reads
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option D. Option A is incorrect because a longer TTL does not matter, because strongly consistent reads are never served from the cache. Option B is incorrect because more nodes add capacity and availability, but the requests still bypass the cache. Option C is incorrect because DAX also passes strongly consistent Query requests through to DynamoDB. Option D is correct because DAX passes strongly consistent reads through to DynamoDB and does not serve them from its cache, so only eventually consistent reads can be cached. Key takeaway: DAX accelerates eventually consistent reads; strongly consistent reads always go to DynamoDB.

questions.question: An SNS topic publishes to an SQS queue in the same account. The queue policy allows sns.amazonaws.com to send messages from the topic ARN. After the team enables SSE-KMS on the queue with the AWS managed key alias/aws/sqs, messages stop arriving and SNS delivery status logs show KMS access denied errors. Company policy requires SSE-KMS with a key that the company controls. What should the developer do?
options: Add a statement for sns.amazonaws.com to the key policy of alias/aws/sqs that allows the required KMS actions
Switch the queue from SSE-KMS to SSE-SQS (SQS-owned keys), so that SNS can deliver without any KMS key policy changes
Add kms:GenerateDataKey and kms:Decrypt statements to the SNS topic's access policy for the queue's encryption key
Use a customer managed KMS key for the queue, with a key policy that allows sns.amazonaws.com to call kms:GenerateDataKey and kms:Decrypt
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option D. Option A is incorrect because AWS managed key policies cannot be modified. Option B is incorrect because this could deliver messages, but the policy requires SSE-KMS with a company-controlled key. Option C is incorrect because KMS permissions are granted in the key policy, and the topic's access policy does not control the use of another resource's key. Option D is correct because SNS must be granted permission to use the queue's key, and only a customer managed key has a key policy that can grant it. Key takeaway: To let an AWS service send to an SSE-KMS encrypted queue, use a customer managed key and grant the service principal kms:GenerateDataKey and kms:Decrypt in its key policy.

questions.question: An ECS service on Fargate runs behind an Application Load Balancer. The application needs about 100 seconds to warm up before its /health endpoint returns 200. The target group checks every 30 seconds with an unhealthy threshold of 2. New tasks are repeatedly stopped and replaced by the ECS service scheduler shortly after they start, although the application would eventually be healthy. What should the developer change?
options: Set the ECS service's health check grace period to a value longer than the warm-up time
Increase the load balancer's idle timeout to 120 seconds so that slow responses are not dropped by the load balancer
Increase the target group's deregistration delay to 120 seconds so that new tasks get more time to become healthy
Reduce the health check interval to 5 seconds so that the load balancer evaluates each new task sooner
questions.explanation: Correct answer: Option A. Option A is correct because during the grace period the scheduler ignores load balancer health check failures, which gives slow-starting tasks time to become healthy. Option B is incorrect because the idle timeout applies to open client connections and does not affect health check evaluation. Option C is incorrect because deregistration delay controls how long in-flight requests can drain when a target is removed, not how long new targets have to start. Option D is incorrect because this makes the load balancer detect failures faster, so the tasks would be replaced even sooner. Key takeaway: Use the ECS health check grace period so that slow-starting tasks are not killed by load balancer health checks before they are ready.

questions.question: A production Lambda function written in Python uses the standard logging module and emits DEBUG logs that inflate CloudWatch Logs costs. The team wants to stop DEBUG output from being ingested in production without changing code, and later wants to search logs by fields such as the request ID in Logs Insights. Which TWO actions should the developer take? (Select TWO)
options: Set the function's application log level to INFO
Set a custom LOG_LEVEL environment variable to INFO
Add a subscription filter that drops DEBUG events
Set only the system log level to WARN
Set the function's log format to JSON
questions.explanation: Correct answers: Option A and Option E. Option A is correct because Lambda then drops application log events below INFO before they are sent to CloudWatch Logs. Option B is incorrect because Lambda does not act on an arbitrary environment variable. It would work only if the code read it and configured the logger. Option C is incorrect because subscription filters forward copies of events to other destinations and do not prevent ingestion or storage. Option D is incorrect because the system log level applies to logs that Lambda generates, such as START and REPORT lines, and not to logs from the function code. Option E is correct because log-level filtering is available only for the JSON log format, and structured JSON logs make fields searchable in Logs Insights. Key takeaway: Lambda advanced logging controls filter application logs by level without code changes, but they require the JSON log format.
